Improvisation in music is the practice of creating melody, harmony, and rhythm spontaneously in real-time performance, either entirely freely or within a structured framework like chord changes, a scale, a raga, or a harmonic progression. Improvisation is the core distinguishing feature of jazz, blues, and Indian classical music, setting these traditions apart from Western concert music, where composition and performance are historically separate activities.

Jazz improvisation builds on a chord progression, the harmonic skeleton, and form—typically twelve-bar blues or jazz-standard changes. Soloists construct new melodic lines over these fixed structures, phrase by phrase. Indian classical music, both Carnatic and Hindustani traditions, improvises within the frameworks of raga—the melodic mode—and tala, the rhythmic cycle. This is not freestyle improvisation but deeply structured improvisation within sophisticated musical grammars.

Improvisation requires internalized knowledge of scales, harmonic progressions, and vocabulary. A jazz musician must know hundreds of melodic phrases, harmonic substitutions, and harmonic movements that can be deployed spontaneously. Blues improvisation centers on bending notes, using call-and-response between vocal and instrumental lines, and exploiting the repetitive twelve-bar structure to develop ideas over multiple choruses.

The greatest improvisers combine technical mastery, deep musical knowledge, and spontaneous creativity. Charlie Parker and John Coltrane in jazz, and Ravi Shankar in Indian music, produced performances that are both structurally coherent and emotionally immediate. Western classical music largely separated composition—creating fixed structures before performance—from performance itself. Improvisation was central to classical music through the eighteenth century but gradually declined in the nineteenth-century concert tradition. Improvisation allows for responsive, interactive music-making; in ensemble improvisation, musicians listen and respond to each other in real time, creating a conversation rather than executing a predetermined plan.
